previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, bipolar disorder, and a history of pseudoseizures was admitted after a syncopal episode and severe abdominal pain. He had run out of pain medication four days prior, which likely contributed to the pain exacerbation. CT imaging showed chronic pancreatitis and gallstones but no acute inflammation or other life-threatening conditions. His pain was controlled with IV and then oral opioids, and he was stabilized on increased doses of long-acting morphine and adjusted insulin due to poor oral intake. The syncopal event was attributed to pain or dehydration rather than a seizure or cardiac cause. He was discharged home with medication changes, instructions to follow up within two weeks, and a plan to evaluate cholecystectomy.
problems: Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Calculus of gallbladder without mention of cholecystitis, without mention of obstruction
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
